title: Why Uruguay Has More Cows Than People
sources: Where Uruguayans live: own count, Kontur Population 2023 (CC BY 4.0) (geo/measure_population.py)
Departments and England: Natural Earth; Rio Grande do Sul regions: IBGE mesorregiões (geo/make_regions.py)
Railway, ship and water arrows drawn through main points (approximate)

paragraphs.text: Uruguay is bigger than England. It has soft green hills, mild winters, good rain, no deserts and no mountains in the way. And it has fewer than three and a half million people. England has more than fifty million.

shots.photo: File:Paisaje del departamento de Río Negro.jpg

paragraphs.text: Now count the cattle. Ranchers in Uruguay declare every animal they own, every year. The last count came to almost twelve million head. That is more than three cows for every person in the country.

shots.on_screen_text: Cattle at La Tablada market, Montevideo, 1920

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 23.jpg

chart.title: Uruguay, 2023-2025 (millions)
chart.source: INE Uruguay, census 2023; MGAP DICOSE declaration 2025 (via Montevideo Portal)

paragraphs.text: And the people are not spread out either. We measured where Uruguayans live, using a population map built from satellite images and census data. Almost half of them live within thirty kilometres of one square in central Montevideo. Half the country lives on a fifth of one percent of its land.

stat.label: Uruguayans living within 30 km of Plaza Independencia
Share of the land where half of Uruguayans live

paragraphs.text: But here is the strange part. Across the border, in the south of Brazil, the same grass rolls on into a state called Rio Grande do Sul. It holds nearly eleven million people. So why is Uruguay so empty? The answer runs through a herd of cattle set loose four hundred years ago, a country designed in London's interest, a law that fenced the countryside, ships that sailed past to Buenos Aires, and families that shrank long before anyone else's. The first reason arrived before the people did.

shots.on_screen_text: The border at Rivera and Santana do Livramento

stat.label: People in Rio Grande do Sul, census 2022

shots.photo: File:A herd of cattle in Uruguay LCCN2016819438.jpg#crop=0.2,0.22,0.2,0.2
shots.on_screen_text: A herd of cattle in Uruguay, about 1918-1920

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea del puerto de Montevideo y la Ciudad Vieja - 0102FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16
File:El Uruguay a través de un siglo page 489 recorte 01.tif#crop=0.03,0.03,0.03,0.13
File:Vista aérea de la bahía de Montevideo - 0086FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

paragraphs.text: Reason one. In the early sixteen hundreds, this coast was the edge of the Spanish empire. On the far bank of the river, the governor of Buenos Aires, Hernando Arias de Saavedra, known as Hernandarias, had a plan for the empty land to the east.

shots.on_screen_text: The eastern bank of the river

paragraphs.text: The dates usually given are 1611 and 1617. Hernandarias sent cattle across the river and let them go on the grassland. Nobody herded them. The grass was endless and the winters were mild.

stat.label: Dates usually given for Hernandarias's cattle
stat.source: INAC; Library of Congress country study

shots.photo: File:Ernesto Laroche - Paisaje de campo con tajamar.jpg

paragraphs.text: A century later, the herds had grown into the millions. The land the Spanish called the Banda Oriental, the eastern bank, became one vast wild ranch. Hunters rode in from Buenos Aires and from Portuguese Brazil to kill cattle for their hides, which were shipped to Europe. Often the hide was all they took.

stat.label: Wild cattle on the eastern bank by the early 1700s

paragraphs.text: Later came the saladeros, salting plants on the riverbanks. Their workers cut the beef into strips, salted it and dried it in the sun. The product was called tasajo. Ships carried it to Brazil and Cuba, where it fed enslaved people on the sugar and coffee plantations. It was the country's first real industry, and it needed cattle, salt and a harbour. It did not need a countryside full of people.

shots.photo: File:Saladero Liebig's - Fray Bentos - Río Negro.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.07,0.3
shots.on_screen_text: The Liebig saladero at Fray Bentos, 1907
Chimney of an old saladero, Salto

shots.photo: File:Vista panorámica - Saladero Liebig's - Río Negro.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.07,0.3
File:Paisaje del departamento de Río Negro.jpg

paragraphs.text: That was the first shape of the country. Not farms and villages, but animals on open grass, and men on horseback who came and went. When Spain and Portugal began to fight over this shore, they built forts, not farms. Portugal founded Colonia del Sacramento in 1680, right across the river from Buenos Aires. Spain answered with a fortress on a fine natural harbour further east. It became a city in 1726. Its name was Montevideo.

shots.on_screen_text: Montevideo Bay and the Cerro from the air

paragraphs.text: Around those forts, the crown handed out the land in huge grants. A single family could hold thousands of hectares. The cattle did the work. So when the time came to make a country, there was already a pattern. A port, a few towns, and empty pasture between them.

shots.photo: File:A herd of cattle in Uruguay LCCN2016819438.jpg#crop=0.2,0.22,0.2,0.2

paragraphs.text: There was one moment when it could have gone differently. In 1815, during the wars of independence, the leader of the eastern bank, José Artigas, issued a land regulation. It ordered the land of his enemies and of the state to be divided up and given out to free Black people, to Indigenous families, to poor creoles and widows. Its most famous line says that the most unfortunate should be the most privileged. A year later, Portuguese troops invaded from Brazil. Artigas was driven into exile in Paraguay, and his land reform was abandoned. The big estates stayed.

shots.photo: File:Juan Manuel Blanes - Artigas en la Ciudadela.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Artigas, painted by Juan Manuel Blanes

shots.photo: File:Ernesto Laroche - Paisaje de campo con tajamar.jpg
File:El Uruguay a través de un siglo page 461 recorte 02.tif#crop=0.03,0.03,0.03,0.13

stat.label: Its principle: the most unfortunate should be the most privileged (1815)

shots.photo: File:Eduardo Carbajal - 1873 - Artigas en el Paraguay.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Artigas in Paraguay, by Eduardo Carbajal, 1873

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Uruguay was not planned by Uruguayans alone. After Artigas fell, the eastern bank was ruled from Rio de Janeiro, first by Portugal and then by the new Empire of Brazil, as its Cisplatine Province. At dawn on the nineteenth of April, 1825, thirty-three exiles led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja crossed the Uruguay River from Argentina and landed on a beach called Agraciada. They raised the countryside against Brazil. Argentina joined in, and the two big neighbours went to war over the eastern bank. Neither could win. Britain, whose merchants wanted the river open for trade, sent a diplomat to broker a peace. His name was Lord Ponsonby.

stat.label: The eastern bank under Portugal, then the Empire of Brazil

paragraphs.text: On the twenty-seventh of August, 1828, the two sides signed a peace convention in Rio de Janeiro. The disputed land would be neither Brazilian nor Argentine. It would be a new, independent state between them. A buffer.

stat.label: Peace convention signed in Rio de Janeiro

paragraphs.text: The new country had one real door to the world, the harbour at Montevideo. Everything that mattered ran through it. The customs house, the merchants, the banks, the government. And the countryside around it was still a place of horsemen and cattle.

shots.photo: File:Ciudad Vieja y puerto de Montevideo - 02493FMHGE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16
File:Vista aérea de la Ciudad Vieja - 0311FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16
File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 17.jpg

paragraphs.text: The young state cleared that countryside in its own way. On the eleventh of April, 1831, the army of President Fructuoso Rivera attacked the Charrúa, the Indigenous people of the plains, at a creek called Salsipuedes. Rivera's own report counted about forty dead and three hundred prisoners, who were handed out to families in Montevideo.

stat.label: Rivera's army attacks the Charrúa at Salsipuedes

shots.photo: File:Juan Manuel Blanes - Retrato del General Fructuoso Rivera.png
shots.on_screen_text: Fructuoso Rivera, by Juan Manuel Blanes

stat.label: Dead and prisoners in Rivera's own report

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea de la Ciudad Vieja - 0310FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

paragraphs.text: Then the country turned on itself. From 1839 to 1851, a civil war known as the Guerra Grande, the Great War, pulled in Argentina, Brazil, Britain and France. For about eight years, Montevideo was under siege. The interior was fought over by riders from both sides, and the herds were slaughtered and stolen.

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 42.jpg

paragraphs.text: When peace finally held, the railways came, built and owned mostly by British companies. The first line opened in 1869. Look at the network on a map. The lines reach out into the cattle country like the ribs of a fan, and every one of them runs back to the same place. The port. Montevideo.

shots.photo: File:El Libro Del Centenario Del Uruguay-page 466-recorte3.tif#crop=0.02,0.02,0.02,0.12
shots.on_screen_text: A cattle wagon of the Central Uruguay Railway, 1925

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea del puerto y la Ciudad Vieja - 0103FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

paragraphs.text: So the country had one door, and the rails pointed to it. But a railway can carry people inland as well as out. Why didn't they go? Because by then, the land itself had been closed.

Reason three. For two hundred years, the grass of the eastern bank had been mostly open. Boundaries were streams, stone walls, hedges of cactus. Cattle wandered, and so did the people who worked them.

shots.on_screen_text: Old stone huts on the grassland

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 34.jpg

paragraphs.text: In the 1860s, sheep arrived in huge numbers, and with them, a demand for order. On the twenty-seventh of July, 1875, a Rural Code came into force. It was written by the ranchers' own association and passed without debate. Landowners now had to mark out their properties. From 1876, imports of fencing wire took off.

stat.label: The Rural Code comes into force

paragraphs.text: Within a generation, the open range was cut into fenced estancias. And a fence changes a ranch. A ranch without fences needs many riders to keep its herds from wandering off. A fenced one needs a few hands to check the wire.

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 60.jpg
File:El Uruguay a través de un siglo page 489 recorte 01.tif#crop=0.03,0.03,0.03,0.13

paragraphs.text: Historians of rural Uruguay describe what came next. Workers who had lived on the ranches were no longer needed. Many drifted to clusters of shacks on the edges of the estates, along the roads and creeks. The ranchers' associations had a name for these places. They called them pueblos de ratas. Rat towns.

shots.on_screen_text: Small settlements on the ranch roads, Tacuarembó

stat.label: "Rat towns": the ranchers' name for the shack settlements

paragraphs.text: The countryside became productive and almost empty at the same time. The last great revolt of the horsemen came from that countryside. In 1904, the rebel leader Aparicio Saravia led thousands of riders against the government. He was shot at the Battle of Masoller on the first of September and died nine days later. It was Uruguay's last civil war. The age of the gaucho was over.

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 42.jpg
File:Desfile militar de Aparicio Saravia el 30 de marzo de 1903.jpg

stat.label: Battle of Masoller: Uruguay's last civil war

paragraphs.text: When industry did come to the cattle, it came to the riverbanks and the port. In the 1860s, the Liebig Extract of Meat Company built a factory at Fray Bentos, on the Uruguay River. It boiled down beef into a dark extract and later canned corned beef that fed European armies. Thousands worked there, and today the site is on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

shots.on_screen_text: Fray Bentos and the old plant
The old plant at Fray Bentos

stat.label: Fray Bentos Industrial Landscape, World Heritage

paragraphs.text: Then came the frozen-meat plants. In 1916 and 1917, the American meatpackers Swift and Armour took over plants on the Cerro, the hill across the bay from Montevideo. Cattle were raised in the empty interior, sent by rail to the capital, and turned into jobs there. The work went to the port, and so did the people.

shots.on_screen_text: The Swift plant on the Cerro, 1918
Meat plants by the Pantanoso creek, 1926

paragraphs.text: So the countryside was closed by the time Europe's great wave of emigrants set sail. And that is where the story gets its sharpest contrast.

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea de la Ciudad Vieja - 0311FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

chapters.title: The Ships Went to Buenos Aires

paragraphs.text: Reason four. Between about 1870 and 1930, some six million Europeans crossed the Atlantic to Argentina. Italians and Spaniards above all. Argentina's immigration law of 1876 offered free lodging on arrival, free train tickets inland and public land on a moving frontier.

shots.photo: File:Immigrant Hotel, Buenos Aires, Argentina LCCN 91739070.tif#crop=0.05,0.07,0.08,0.11
shots.on_screen_text: The Immigrants' Hotel, Buenos Aires, early 1900s

shots.photo: File:Hotel de Inmigrantes c. 1912 - Google Arts & Culture.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Immigrants' Hotel, Buenos Aires, about 1912

paragraphs.text: Uruguay got far fewer. Estimates for the half century after 1880 run from under three hundred thousand to nearly six hundred thousand. And most of the newcomers who did come stayed exactly where the ship docked. In 1889, almost half the people of Montevideo had been born abroad.

arrows.label: Most ships sail on to Buenos Aires

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea de la bahía de Montevideo - 0086FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

shots.on_screen_text: Immigrants at the Isla de Flores quarantine station, 1921

shots.photo: File:C25f241. Muelle de entrada para control de inmigrantes.jpg

paragraphs.text: Italians were the largest group, nearly half of all foreigners in the capital. Even in 1908, when the whole country was counted, about one person in six had been born abroad. Most of them lived in Montevideo.

shots.on_screen_text: The immigrant quarantine station, Isla de Flores

shots.photo: File:Ciudad Vieja y puerto de Montevideo - 02493FMHGE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

paragraphs.text: The reason was the same fence. Out in the interior there was no frontier to claim. The good land was already held, in units of thousands of hectares, by families who did not need more workers. An Italian peasant could find work in Montevideo's port and workshops. He could not find a farm.

shots.photo: File:El Uruguay a través de un siglo page 461 recorte 02.tif#crop=0.03,0.03,0.03,0.13

paragraphs.text: Now look across the border again. In 1824, the first German families arrived at São Leopoldo, in the forested hills of northern Rio Grande do Sul. From 1875, Italians followed, about a hundred thousand of them before the First World War, most of them to the highlands around a new colony that became the city of Caxias do Sul. They were given family-sized lots, cleared the forest and built farming villages, then towns, then cities.

shots.on_screen_text: Centenary of German settlement, São Leopoldo, 1924

shots.photo: File:Caxias do Sul - RS, Brazil - panoramio.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The hills around Caxias do Sul

shots.photo: File:Igreja de Caxias do Sul em 1883. (6615475477).jpg
File:Amadeo Rossi & Cia - Caxias do Sul, RS - 1932.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Plan of the Jaguari colony lots, 1898
Vineyards in the Serra Gaúcha, Gramado

paragraphs.text: We split Rio Grande do Sul into its official regions and measured them with the same population map. In the southwest, on the open pampa along Uruguay's border, the old cattle country, there are about eleven people per square kilometre. In the northeast, the hills of the old colonies, there are forty-seven. In Uruguay's interior, away from the southern coast, there are about seven.
So the grass is not the reason. On the Brazilian side, the cattle country is almost as empty as Uruguay's. The people are where small farmers were given land. Uruguay never had that frontier.

shots.photo: File:Border between Rivera and Santana do Livramento.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Gramado, in the old colony hills

shots.photo: File:El Embajador de los Estados Unidos, Lou Rinaldi, participó en Tacuarembó del desfile de la 39a Fiesta de la Patria Gaucha en 14 Marzo 2026 - 33.jpg

paragraphs.text: Still, a country can fill up slowly from within, if its families are large. Uruguay's were not.

Reason five. Uruguay changed its family life decades before the rest of Latin America. Demographers count it among the first countries in the region to see both death rates and birth rates fall, at least thirty years ahead of its neighbours.

stat.label: Uruguay's head start in the demographic transition

paragraphs.text: Part of that was a country turning secular and urban early. A large share of the people lived in one city, with jobs, schools and newspapers, far from the large rural families of the interior. In the early nineteen hundreds, under President José Batlle y Ordóñez, the state separated from the church. Divorce became legal in 1907. A few years later, a wife could end a marriage simply because she wished to.

shots.photo: File:Vista aérea del Puerto y la Ciudad Vieja - 0017FMHE.tif#crop=0.07,0.07,0.06,0.16

paragraphs.text: By 1950, Uruguayan women had on average about two point seven children. Most of Latin America did not reach that level until the end of the century. Brazil and Argentina grew through the twentieth century, while Uruguay's population grew slowly.

chart.title: Children per woman
chart.source: Cabella et al.; Nathan, Pardo & Cabella

paragraphs.text: The country aged with it. In 1963, fewer than one Uruguayan in twelve was sixty-five or older. In the 2023 census it was about one in six, and the statistics office expects one in three by 2070.
And the fall never stopped. By 2021, the rate was down to about one point four children per woman, far below the two needed to keep a population level. Every new generation is smaller than the last.
A country with small families can still grow if people arrive. Uruguay had the opposite problem. Its people left.

Reason six. In 1973, the military took power in Uruguay. Over the next twelve years, thousands were jailed for their politics. By the time democracy returned in 1985, about three hundred and eighty thousand people had left the country. In a nation of about three million, that was more than one person in ten.

shots.photo: File:Asunción a la Presidencia de la Republica de Juan María Bordaberry - 11442FMHGE (cropped).tif
shots.on_screen_text: Juan María Bordaberry takes office, 1 March 1972
Square of the 1973 General Strike, Montevideo
Silent march for the disappeared, Montevideo, 2024
Silent march for the disappeared, Montevideo, 2024

paragraphs.text: Then, in 2002, a banking crisis spread from Argentina. Banks closed their doors, and between 1999 and 2002 about a hundred thousand more people left. Studies found that the ones leaving were often the ones with university degrees.
They went to Buenos Aires, to Spain, to the United States. Today there are hundreds of thousands of Uruguayans abroad.

The latest census, in 2023, counted three point five million people, only a little more than twelve years earlier. The national statistics office said that without immigrants, the population would have fallen. Even Montevideo is getting smaller. The capital lost about five percent of its people between the two counts, as families moved out to the coast and suburbs nearby.

Living in one corner has its risks. In 2023, after a record drought, the main reservoir for the capital, Paso Severino on the Santa Lucía River, fell to a few percent of its capacity. More than half the country drinks from that one river system. For months, the water company mixed salty water from the River Plate estuary into the supply, and people in Montevideo opened their taps to water that tasted of salt. The crisis ended only when the rains came back in late August.

shots.on_screen_text: Headquarters of OSE, the water company

paragraphs.text: So the people who might have filled the interior never came, and many of those who were born there went somewhere else. But the interior is not standing still. Something is growing on the old ranches.

Our population map shows how lopsided it has become. The six departments along the southern coast hold seven in ten Uruguayans on less than a fifth of the land. In Durazno and Flores, in the middle of the country, there are fewer than five people per square kilometre. Montevideo, the smallest department of all, holds well over a million.

shots.photo: File:Casa de la Cultura, Durazno, Uruguay.jpg

paragraphs.text: Drive north from Montevideo today and you will see it. Long straight rows of eucalyptus, planted where cattle used to graze. More than a million hectares of the country are now pine and eucalyptus plantations.

stat.label: Pine and eucalyptus plantations in Uruguay, 2023

paragraphs.text: The sheep that once came with the fences are going too. In the late 1980s, Uruguay had about twenty-five million of them. By 2025, the flock had fallen to under five million, as pasture went to crops, cattle and trees.

In April 2023, a Finnish company, UPM, started a new pulp mill at Paso de los Toros, in the middle of the country. It can produce two point one million tonnes of pulp a year, from trees grown on the old grassland. And on the hilltops, wind turbines turn. In 2024, almost all of Uruguay's electricity came from renewable sources, more than a quarter of it from wind.

shots.on_screen_text: The UPM mill at Paso de los Toros
UPM mill, Paso de los Toros

stat.label: Pulp a year from the Paso de los Toros mill

paragraphs.text: But planted forests and wind farms, like cattle ranches, cover a great deal of land with very few workers. The interior is producing more than ever, and it is still nearly empty.

shots.on_screen_text: The UPM mill at Fray Bentos

shots.photo: File:Planta de celulosa de UPM II 12.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The UPM mill at Paso de los Toros

shots.photo: File:Planta de celulosa de UPM II 26.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: UPM pulp mill, Paso de los Toros

paragraphs.text: The cows came first, on open grass. The country was built around one port. Fences closed the land, the ships sailed past to Buenos Aires, the families were small, and in hard times the young left. None of these alone would empty a country. Together, they made a nation that lives on its southern coast and keeps its interior for cattle, trees and wind.

paragraphs.text: Would you trade a city flat for a house in Uruguay's quiet interior, with more cows than neighbours? Tell me in the comments.

youtube.description: Uruguay is bigger than England, with mild winters, good rain and endless grass, yet it has fewer than 3.5 million people and almost 12 million cattle. Half of all Uruguayans live within 30 km of one square in Montevideo. Across the border, the same grass in southern Brazil holds nearly 11 million. We follow the answer from orbit and the archives: cattle set loose in the 1600s, a buffer state with one port, the Rural Code and the fences of 1875, the emigrant ships that sailed on to Buenos Aires, families that shrank decades early, the exiles of 1973 and 2002, and the eucalyptus, pulp mills and wind farms on the old ranches.
